question.text: Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that $\displaystyle \int_2^b f(x)\, \textrm d x = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left[\left(2 + \dfrac{5k}{n}\right)^2\cdot \dfrac 5 n\right].$
question.explanation:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows: \[ \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm d x = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f\left(x_k\right)\cdot \Delta x \] where $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_k = a + k\Delta x.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=2.$

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $\Delta x = \dfrac{5}{n}.$ Therefore, \[ \dfrac{5}{n} = \dfrac{b-2}{n} \quad\Longrightarrow \quad b=7. \]

Consequently, $x_k = 2 + \dfrac{5k}{n}$ and $f(x_k) = x_k^2.$

Hence, \[ \int_{2}^{7} x^2\, \textrm d x = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left[\left(2 + \dfrac{5k}{n}\right)^2\cdot \dfrac 5 n\right]. \]

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)= x^2$ and $b = 7.$

example.title: Expressing the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum as a Definite Integral

question.text: What is $\displaystyle\int_{e}^{3e} \ln{x} \,\textrm d x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
question.explanation:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

\[ \int_a^b f(x)\textrm{d}x = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} f(x_i) \cdot \Delta x, \]

where $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_i = a + i\Delta x.$

In the definite integral

\[ \int_{e}^{3e} \ln{x} \,\textrm d x, \]

the function is $f(x) = \ln{x},$ the lower bound is $a=e,$ and the upper bound is $b=3e.$ So, we have

\[ \Delta x = \dfrac{3e-e}{n} = \dfrac{2e}{n}, \]

and therefore

\begin{align*} \int_{e}^{3e} \ln{x}\,\textrm d x &= \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} f(x_i) \cdot \Delta x \\[5pt] &= \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \left[f\left( e + i\cdot \dfrac{2e} n \right) \cdot \dfrac{2e} n\right] \\[5pt] &= \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \left[f\left( e + \dfrac {2ie}{n} \right) \cdot \dfrac{2e} n\right] \\[5pt] &= \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \left[\ln\left(e + \dfrac{2ie}{n}\right)\cdot \dfrac{2e} n\right]. \end{align*}

example.title: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum

question.text: What is $\displaystyle\int_{2}^{4} (x+1)^2 \, \textrm{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
question.explanation:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as \[ \int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} f(x_i) \cdot \Delta x, \]

where $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_i = a + i\Delta x.$

In the definite integral \[ \int_{2}^{4} (x+1)^2 \, \textrm{d}x, \] the function is $f(x) = (x+1)^2,$ the lower bound is $a=2,$ and the upper bound is $b=4.$ So, we have \[ \Delta x = \dfrac{4-2}{n} = \dfrac{2}{n}, \]

and therefore \begin{align} \int_{2}^{4} (x+1)^2 \, \textrm d x & = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} f(x_i) \cdot \Delta x \\[5pt] & = \lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\left[f\left(2 + i\cdot \dfrac{2}{n}\right)\,\cdot \dfrac{2}{n}\right]\\[5pt] &= \lim_{n \to \infty}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \left[ f\left(2 + \dfrac{2 i}{n}\right) \cdot \dfrac{2}{n}\right] \\[5pt] & = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\left[ \left(2 + \dfrac{2 i}{n} + 1 \right)^2 \cdot \dfrac{2}{n}\right]\\[5pt] & = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\left[ \left(3 + \dfrac{2 i}{n} \right)^2 \cdot \dfrac{2}{n}\right]. \end{align}

example.title: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum

question.text: What is $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} e^{x} \, \textrm d x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
question.explanation:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as \[ \int_{a}^{b} f(x) \,\textrm d x = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{k = 1}^n f(x_k) \cdot \Delta x, \] where $x_k = a + k\Delta x$ and $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral \[ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{2} e^{x} \, \textrm d x, \] the function is $f(x) = e^{x},$ the lower bound is $a=0$ and the upper bound is $b=2.$ So, we have \[ \Delta x = \dfrac{2-0}{n} = \dfrac{2}{n}. \]

Therefore, \begin{align} \int_{0}^{2} e^{x} \, \textrm d x & = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^n f(x_k) \cdot \Delta x\\[5pt] & = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^n \left[ f\left(0 + k \cdot \dfrac{2}{n}\right) \cdot \dfrac{2}{n}\right]\\[5pt] & = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^n\left[ f\left(\dfrac{2k}{n}\right) \cdot \dfrac{2}{n}\right] \\[5pt] & = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^n\left[ e^{2k/n} \cdot \dfrac{2}{n}\right]. \end{align}

example.title: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Right Riemann Sum

question.text: Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that $\displaystyle\int_2^b f(x)\, \textrm d x = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left[4\left(2 + \dfrac{k}{n}\right)^3\cdot \dfrac{1}{n}\right].$
question.explanation:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows: \[ \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm d x = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f\left(x_k\right)\cdot \Delta x \] where $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_k = a + k\Delta x.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=2.$

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $\Delta x = \dfrac{1}{n}.$ Therefore, \[ \dfrac{1}{n} = \dfrac{b-2}{n} \quad\Longrightarrow \quad b=3. \]

Consequently, $x_k = 2 + \dfrac{k}{n}$ and $f(x_k) = 4x_k^3.$

Hence, \[ \int_2^3 4x^3 \, \textrm d x = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left[4\left(2 + \dfrac{k}{n}\right)^3\cdot \dfrac{1}{n}\right]. \]

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)= 4x^3$ and $b=3.$
